story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Mommy passed her a bowl of soup. Aubrey saw the orange soup with her eyes. She smelled it with her nose. Sniff, sniff. It smelled warm and sweet.

Aubrey had a problem. Her spoon was too far away. "Mommy, pass the spoon, please," she said. Mommy passed it right to her hand. Aubrey touched the warm bowl with her fingers. Then she tasted the soup with her tongue.

One bite, two bites, three bites. Yum. "I heard the kitty purr with my ears," Aubrey said. "Lucky kitty. Lucky me." The kitty purred by her chair.

Livia walked into the big art room with Mommy. There were paintings on every wall. A lady with a paint smock smiled at her. "Would you like to try painting?" she asked. Livia wanted to make a flower for Grandma. She pointed at three little jars. "This one is red," said Livia. "This is yellow. That is blue." The lady nodded and set out a paper and a brush. Livia painted a red stem. Then she painted yellow petals around it. She wanted an orange flower next. She dipped her brush in the red jar and then the yellow jar. On her paper, the two colors swirled together and turned orange. Livia laughed out loud and made a big noise. "I made orange! Red and yellow chase each other and make orange!" "You did it," said Mommy, hugging her. The lady let Livia take the painting home for Grandma. Livia carried it with both hands, careful not to smudge the orange.

Thomas wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He climbed up on the little stool by the sink. Mommy was right there, folding a towel. Thomas turned the knob on the left. The water came out warm. He put his hands under it. Then he turned the knob on the right too. Whoosh! The water got very hot. "Ow!" said Thomas, and pulled his hands back fast. The hot water made his hands hurt. Mommy hurried over. "I forgot," Thomas said. "Hot water is not for hands." Mommy held his rough little hands under cool water. Slowly the hurt went away. Thomas turned only the left knob this time. The water felt just right. "We did it together," Mommy said, and they washed until his hands were clean.

Cooper found one big red ball in the playroom. He wanted to roll it down the stairs. Mommy said, "Take turns with Anna. First Cooper, then Anna." Cooper rolled the ball. It bounced down and slipped under the sofa. Anna had a long spoon. She pushed the ball out with the spoon. "My turn now," said Anna. Cooper gave her the ball. Anna rolled it and it slipped under the chair this time. Cooper used the spoon to get it out. "Now my turn again," said Cooper. They took turns all afternoon. Outside, the street was wet from the rain. Through the window Cooper watched the drops fall. Then he rolled the ball to Anna, and she rolled it back.

Sara went to the library with Mommy. She wanted a book about bunnies. She saw a boy crying by the blocks. His tower had fallen down. Sara sat next to him. "I can help," she said. They built the tower again together. The boy stopped crying and smiled. Sara smiled too.

Sara found the bunny books. A girl was reading one already. Sara felt her face get hot. She wanted to grab it. But she waited and counted to ten. Soon the girl gave her the book. Sara felt happy inside.

Then Sara heard a loud thunder sound. It was just the big door closing. She jumped and held Mommy's hand. Mommy hugged her tight. Sara looked at her bunny book and got excited. "Bunnies hop wild in the yard at the store by our house," she told Mommy. She hugged the book and hopped like a bunny to the door.

Yesterday it rained at daycare. Declan had to play inside all day. He wanted to paint the big paper sun outside.

Today Declan runs to the window. The ground is dry. The sun feels warm on his hand. "Can we go outside now?" he asks. His teacher smiles. "Yes, now," she says.

Declan finds his glue stick on the little table. His problem was that the sun shape kept slipping. The glue stick helps it stay. He sticks the yellow sun onto his paper. It is different from yesterday's paper, because today the sun is dry and flat.

Later they will water the plants. But right now Declan pats his sun softly. It does not move. "Tomorrow I will make a moon," he says, and presses the glue stick down one more time.

Charlie put her bread in the toaster. Pop! The toast jumped out. It was warm.

"Mama, I want to make it myself," Charlie said. She held the knife with both hands. She pushed the butter on the toast. It went slide, slide, slide off. "Why did it slip?" Charlie asked. Then she looked closer. "Because my butter was too thin! It slid off like a flower petal floats away."

Charlie scooped a big thick dab of butter. She pressed it. It stayed! She spread it slowly. One, two, three, all the way to the edge.

Next came the milk. Charlie tipped the cup first, just a little. The milk slid down the side. Pour, pour, pour. Not one drop on the table!

"Look, Mama! Toast and milk, all done by me."

"You did it," Mama said. "Want a bite?"

Charlie smiled and took a big, buttery bite.

Madeline ran up the porch of Grandma's house. Her shoes went clack, clack on the steps. Inside, the whole room smelled like warm cake. Balloons bobbed on the ceiling.

On the table sat a big white cake with five pink candles. Grandma said the candles had to wait. Madeline wanted to blow them out right now. She leaned close and puffed her cheeks. "Not yet, sweet pea," said Grandma. "The friends are still coming."

More friends came in. They sat on every chair and little stool. Then everyone sang the birthday song, loud and silly. Grandpa struck a match and lit each candle. The flames made the cake glow. Madeline took a big breath and blew. All the candles went dark, and smoke curled up like a little gray snake. Everyone clapped and cheered.

Grandma cut the first slice for Madeline. The cake inside was cool and pink, with sweet jam in the middle. Madeline looked at the smoke-gray snakes rising from the candles and whispered, "The fire made the smoke." She took a big, sweet bite.

Maria wanted to pick the apples in the backyard. There was one big red apple on the tree. She reached up high. The apple was too far away.

"Stay close to me," said Mommy. Maria stood right by Mommy's side. Mommy got the step stool. Maria held it steady. Mommy picked the apple. It was cold from the shade. Maria wiped it on her shirt. Then she took a big bite. It was sweet and crunchy.

Near the fence was the grill. It was Daddy's new grill. Maria walked toward it. Mommy said, "The grill is hot. Hot can hurt." Maria could feel warm air on her hand. She jumped back fast. "The grill is hot," she said. "Hot, hot!" She put her sun hat back on her head. Then she sat with Mommy and ate her apple all gone.

Alice went to the store with her mom. Her little brother was in the cart. He was hungry and wanted apples. Mom said, "Please get six apples, Alice." Alice put apples in the bag. She said the number words as she went. "One, two, three, four, five." The bag felt too light. Alice looked inside. She counted again, slow this time. "One, two, three, four, five." There were only five apples. "The bag has five because I stopped at five," she said. She tried one more apple. "Six!" Now the bag felt just right. Alice gave the apples to Mom. Her brother grabbed one and took a big bite. Alice smiled and said, "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

Lydia held Daddy's hand in the big stadium. Everyone sat in long rows of seats. The game was about to start. Lydia's tummy felt jumpy and excited.

The players ran out onto the green field. Lydia clapped all by herself. "One clap, two claps, three claps," she counted. But her claps were too small to hear. Then the team scored a goal! Mommy clapped. Grandma clapped. Her friend Ben clapped. Lydia clapped with them. "One clap, two claps, three claps," they counted together. The claps were big and loud, like thunder. Lydia smiled. "Our claps got loud because we clapped together!" she said. The game went on and on. In the last minute, the team scored again. Lydia stood up on her seat and skipped in place. "One clap, two claps, three claps," she counted. The whole stadium clapped with her.

Emilia wanted a shiny red ball at the store. There was only one red ball left. A little boy picked it up at the same time. Emilia reached out her hand too. The boy held the ball tight. Mom said, "There are many balls here. Let's look together."

Emilia and the boy looked at the shelf. Emilia found a green ball. She gave it to the boy. "You can have this one," she said. The boy smiled. He put down the red ball. He picked up the green ball.

Emilia put the red ball in the cart. "I want this present for my birthday," she said. Mom put it deep in the cart with the bread. Emilia waved bye-bye to the boy. He waved back and bounced his green ball.

Chloe stood in the kitchen with Mommy. Mommy held a big red apple.

"Name my five senses," Mommy said. "You win a bite."

Chloe thought hard. "Eyes see!" she said.

"Good," said Mommy.

" ears hear!" Chloe said.

"Almost. Say it right."

"Ears hear! Nose smells!" Chloe sniffed the apple. "Mmm!"

"Taste next," said Mommy.

"Tongue tastes!" said Chloe.

"Last one," said Mommy.

Chloe patted her hands and then her back. "Skin feels!" she said.

"You win!" Mommy laughed. She stopped cutting the apple and gave Chloe a slice.

Chloe took a big bite. Crunch, crunch. "It's crunchy!" she said. "My ears hear crunch. My tongue tastes sweet. My skin feels cold juice. I used all five senses!"

"Smart girl," said Mommy. Chloe took another crunchy bite.

Andrew stood at the edge of the pool. He was a little shy. The water looked big and blue.

"Come in, Andrew," said Mom. She held his hand. Andrew put one foot in. Then the other. The water felt warm.

"Now hold the edge and kick," said Mom. Andrew kicked. Nothing happened. He stopped and waited. Then he tried again. He kicked harder. He popped up and moved forward!

"I moved! My legs pushed me!" said Andrew. "The water is easy to push."

He kicked all the way to the steps. "You worked hard," said Mom. "Now time for a nap."

Andrew smiled and got out. He waved bye-bye to the water.

Chloe wanted toast like Mommy's toast, with yellow butter all over it. She held the little knife in her hand. The butter was cold and hard. The knife slid and slipped right off the toast. Chloe made a face. Then she pushed the butter with slow, small pushes. The butter got soft and warm. It spread like paint. "I did it!" Chloe said.

Next came the milk. She held the cup with both hands. She poured very slowly. The milk came out in a tiny line. "Go slow and it stays in," Chloe whispered. The cup filled up. Not one drop on the table.

Daddy peeked in. "Yum, can I have some?" Chloe laughed and pushed the cup far away. "This is my stormy-day snack, all mine!" She took a big crunchy bite.

Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. She held her teddy bear tight. The nurse came in with a tiny shot. "Will it hurt?" Emilia asked. "Just a little pinch," the nurse said. Emilia looked at the needle. It was so small. "Why is it so tiny?" she asked. "Because it only needs a little bit," the nurse said. Emilia held out her arm. The nurse drew a small line on her skin. "Count with me," the nurse said. "One, two, three!" Emilia counted fast. Pinch! It was over. Emilia blinked. "That was it?" she asked. "Yes, all done," the nurse said. Emilia hugged her bear. She gave him a weak arm right after, then flexed it strong. "I was brave!" she said. She skipped out the door with her sticker.

Scarlett was tired. She wanted to help Mommy make soup. She stood on a chair near the stove. Steam rose up from the pot.

"Stop," said Mommy. "Come to me." Scarlett jumped down. She stood close to Mommy's leg. Mommy let her hold the spoon handle for one little second. The metal was warm. Scarlett said, "The fire makes the pot hot. So I stand back." Mommy smiled and nodded.

Then Scarlett rolled an orange across the table to Mommy. Mommy rolled it back. They waited while the soup bubbled. At last it was time to eat. Scarlett sat in her chair at the table. She blew on her spoon, one, two, three. Then she took a small taste. The soup was just right. Scarlett rolled one more orange to Mommy and grinned.

Nora wanted to go outside and see the snow. Mommy said, "First put on your coat." Nora tried to zip it up, but the zipper would not move. Then she saw the little teeth. The zipper had to go all the way down first. Nora pushed the two sides together at the very bottom. Zip, zip, zip! It went up all by itself. "I did it!" Nora said. One arm in, two arms in, three zips up. Outside, the snow was soft and cold. Nora pretended she was a loud sheep. Baa, baa, baa! Her cold nose made Mommy laugh, and Mommy zipped the collar up one more zip.

Amelia ran into the library. She loved the big shelves of books. Today she wanted a dinosaur book. She found one with a big green dinosaur on the front.

Amelia held the book tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Her mother smiled. "Look at the last page," she said. Amelia opened the book at the back. There was a stamp with a date on it. "That is the day it goes back," said her mother.

Amelia made a sad face. "But the dinosaur will be lonely," she said. Her mother laughed. "Another boy or girl wants to read it too," she said. Amelia looked at the front of the book. She saw small black words under the picture. "What are these?" she asked. "Words tell the story," said her mother. "Read them from the front to the last page."

At home, Amelia read the book with her mother. The words made the dinosaur roar and stomp. On the last page, the dinosaur waved goodbye. "Bye-bye, dinosaur," Amelia said. She waved back.

Miles ran into the library. He wanted to draw on the little tablet. It hung on a hook by the desk, quiet and still. He pressed the round button. The screen glowed. "It woke up!" Miles said. He tapped a yellow picture of a crayon. A drawing app opened, white and blank. Miles made a big blue bus. Then he made the sun.

"I want to draw again tomorrow," Miles said. But where did the drawing go? He looked at the screen. His blue bus was there, saved inside the tablet. He had pressed save, so it stayed. Miles pressed the button again. The screen went dark and sleepy.

Miles carried it back. It was not heavy at all. He hung it gently on the hook. "Good night, tablet," he whispered, and waved goodbye to his bus.
